Steam is a wonderful service, as is GOG, but they both have very different business philosophies and average target audiences. I don't think that GOG will outright replace Steam, but GOG building itself up as a major digital distributor would be the sort of competition that would really motivate Valve to start improving Steam as a service. You can't justify the effort involved in improving your service when you have a virtual monopoly on digital PC game distribution, but GOG building itself up as a major player and addressing the common complaints about Steam would force Valve to start improving the service lest they lose users. In the end, I welcome any significant competition in this market, because it will force everyone involved to get off their behinds and start improving their service, which can only be a good thing in my view.

I sincerely doubt GOG will ever replace, usurp, or unseat, or any other verb to steam. What it will do however is keep them honest, and keep them from getting away with whatever they want. GOG is increasingly a viable alternative to Steam, without the DRM, the greenlight garbage, the microtransactions on hats and cards. Plus, IMHO, GOG is more attractive to developers because it's more exclusive, games go on sale less, and games sell for more even when they are on sale. Your game retains more value on GOG than on Steam, which has turned into a race to the bottom.

Now, the price of your game on GOG still has to compete with the price of your game on Steam. However, GOG is typically better about extras, support, and compatibility. Those things might not be relevant to your game specifically, but the overall perceived value add of GOG is still there.

The downside is that GOG seems to do less to promote individual games (that aren't The Witcher), and their website as a whole is just less of a community hub than Steam is.

You have some valid points, though there was something written by a small developer earlier this year, talking about the effect Steam sales (whether major events or a sporadic choice by a developer) on daily/weekly income. It was only one person of course, but his final word on the matter was that, despite the reduced income, the sales increase does tend to result in larger earning during a sale period. Which makes sense. After all, ten sales at $10 are good, but a hundred sales at $5 are better y'know?

That is broadly true. Study after study has shown that sales increase short term profit and revenue.

But there is the unstudied long term effects of devaluing games. Although you occasionally do see people who've been making games for decades lamenting how the margins just keep getting smaller and smaller, and Steam has turned things into a race to the bottom. I believe the guy who did Revenge of the Titans did a few very controversial blog posts ranting about how each customer is only worth pennies to your average indie dev, so customer service and trying to actually cater to anyways goes completely to the wayside.

Jonathan Blow also spoke quite critically about sales as I recall. It's certainly an issue that requires further study. However, I remain unconvinced that it's an entirely, categorically bad thing for everyone. I think, personal opinion so not based on anything other than subjective observation, that the "race to the bottom" is based more on people who are making games that aren't as good as they think they are. Now fighting to make their name in a market that's far more competitive, with games that are significantly better than used to be, even when made on miniscule budgets. Where, in the past, the games we now consider average, at best, were the best in a comparative bunch. Because, notice, it's a "problem" that doesn't just affect niche Indie devs. Massive budget, hugely advertised games that are lacklustre and dull are also rewarded with poor sales. Like Colonial Marines for example

My only fear with the "more competition the better" stuff is that smaller players and a more busy market like that opens more risk for some players not making it or going under and as a result what then happens to the content/licenses. For better or for worse I trust that steam will be around in a few years should I want to download and play a game I bought because Valve is a big, more financially stable, viable juggernaut/monopoly more than I'd trust a smaller competitor or startup.
